title: Rotating a Toilet to an ADA-Height, 14-Inch Rough-In with Flange Adaptation

locations.name: Probable residential bathroom (interior, with tile floor and toilet flange)
locations.basis: Transcript centers on a home bathroom installation: references to the closet flange, tile floor, and a basement water line imply a house bathroom setup; no explicit shooting location provided.

summary: This Old House demonstrates how to rotate a toilet to achieve a more natural angle and ADA-ready height in a residential bathroom. The segment covers measuring for a standard 12-inch rough-in, reporting a 14-inch distance from the back wall to the bolt holes when repositioned, and upgrading to a taller, 18-inch finish-floor height for better accessibility. When the existing flange lacks a usable keyway, the host selects a flange adapter solution, installs a wax seal, and anchors the base into tile with masonry anchors and bolts. The water supply is adapted with a longer flexible line to avoid re-piping, and the unit is tested for a successful, low-flow flush (about 1.3 gpf compared to the old toilet’s higher usage). The procedure emphasizes precise bolt alignment (parallel to the back wall), even tightening, and proper seal to prevent leaks.

sections.title: Problem framing and objective
concepts: goal: rotate toilet to a more natural angle
consideration of wheelchair access and orientation

sections.description: The presenter outlines the problem: the toilet seems to be facing the wrong way and the homeowners want a more natural angle, with accessibility considerations noted.

sections.title: Toilet rough-in basics and 14-inch back-to-wall dimension
concepts: 12-inch standard rough-in from wall to pipe center
14-inch back-to-wall distance for bolt holes when rotated
measurements to confirm new toilet fit
sections.description: A primer on toilets 101: the standard rough-in is 12 inches, and a rotated configuration would place the bolts about 14 inches from the back wall. The host demonstrates measuring these distances to anticipate how a new toilet will seal to the floor and wall without gaps.

sections.title: ADA-height considerations and new toilet height
concepts: old toilet seat height vs new height
finish-floor height around 18 inches
ADA-compliance for wheelchair use
sections.description: The new toilet is compared to the old one: the finish height increases from about 16 inches to roughly 18 inches, improving accessibility and ADA compliance for wheelchair users.

sections.title: Removal of the old toilet
concepts: water off and toilet removal
placing the old toilet on a drop cloth/newspaper
removal of the wax ring
sections.description: The old toilet is drained, lifted straight up, and set aside. The wax ring is removed to expose the closet flange for inspection.

sections.title: Flange evaluation and compatibility issues
concepts: existing flange lacks keyway
difference between old and modern flanges
incompatibility of the old flange with standard bolts
sections.description: The video reveals that the existing flange has no keyway for new bolts and cannot be swapped for a modern flange without adaptation.

sections.title: Flange adaptation options
concepts: adapter to create new keyway on the existing flange
alternative wax-seal-based approach to securing new bolts
sections.description: Two approaches are discussed to enable bolt insertion: a flange adapter that creates new keyways and a wax-seal-based method that anchors a new bolt pattern into the floor and flange interface.

sections.title: Wax ring prep and initial seating
concepts: wax ring cut in half for sealing
positioning the wax ring for flush seating
ensuring bolts are parallel to the back wall
sections.description: A half wax ring is used to create a proper seal, then bolts are lined up parallel to the back wall before final seating.

sections.title: Drilling into tile and securing with anchors
concepts: drilling into tile with a masonry bit
installing masonry anchor screws and tightening evenly
avoidance of over-tightening
sections.description: The base is anchored to the floor by drilling into tile and inserting masonry anchors; screws are tightened evenly to avoid over-torquing.

sections.title: Water supply relocation concept

use of longer flexible supply rather than re-piping from basement
planning to route behind the toilet
sections.description: The existing supply line location is described, with a plan to use a longer flexible line to connect to the new toilet rather than running a new line from the basement.

sections.title: Final assembly: mounting, washers, and connections
concepts: connection hardware orientation: brass washer, nut, and washer direction
snugging bolts evenly on both sides
sections.description: The supply line and toilet are mounted, with careful attention to washer orientation and even tightening to ensure a solid seal without overtightening.

sections.title: Performance and test flush

contrast with the old one-piece toilet that used roughly five gallons per flush
homeowner test flush
sections.description: After installation, the toilet is filled and tested. The new unit uses about 1.3 gallons per flush, a significant reduction from the previous inefficient one-piece toilet; the homeowner performs the test flush in the closing segment.
